Related-work name-drops kept only where relied upon (Jakesch opinion bias; Bai/Song RLHF entropy; Kleinberg monoculture framing).

extractionFlags.scope_walls: eight-sentence English microfiction; three adventure topics; non-professional UK Prolific writers/readers; GPT-4 at study time
extractionFlags.construct_adaptation: usefulness redefined toward YA appropriateness / book developability / publisher likelihood
extractionFlags.exploratory_vs_preregistered: ownership, profit split, ethics, disclosure are exploratory (S5); emotional characteristics partly exploratory
extractionFlags.self_vs_other: writer self-ratings null across conditions while evaluator ratings move

papers.extractor_notes: Science Advances online experiment: N=293 UK Prolific writers (8-sentence YA microfiction; GPT-4 three-sentence idea opt-in; Human-only vs 1 vs ≤5 ideas) and N=600 evaluators (3519 ratings). Preregistered novelty/usefulness; similarity via OpenAI embeddings; DAT heterogeneity; ownership/ethics exploratory (S5). Intention-to-treat; 88.4% GenAI take-up. No skill-implication nodes.

Published Science Advances OCR only (same study as kobak-academic-2024 preprint — do not dual-corroborate). Corpus-level excess-vocabulary design; no per-abstract detection. Numbers from abstract/results: Δ=0.135 lower bound; COVID content Δ=0.069; subcorpus peaks to ~0.40+.

CHI 2023 / arXiv 2302.00560. Online experiment N=1,506 writers + N=500 judges; GPT-3 davinci-002 writing assistant opinionated via invisible prefix+infix prompts on 'Is social media good for society?'. Core claims: written-opinion shift and post-task attitude shift (latent persuasion), with low awareness. Mechanisms discussed as informational / normative / behavioral; gaps on topic generalizability, persistence, and weaker deployed opinions.

Science Advances 2026; two preregistered Prolific experiments (Exp1 N=1485 standardized tests; Exp2 N=1097 four partisan issues with pre–post ~34 days). GPT-3.5/GPT-4 autocomplete biased by design. Capture attitude-shift main effects, unawareness, Static Text vs autocomplete, Write-in-Favor benchmark, and Warning/Debrief safeguards that fail. No skill-implication nodes.

PARTIAL OCR (~67k words / 216pp metadata). Extracted from abstract, intro RQ framing, experimental design, interview/ownership/quoting results, NLP discussion, EEG summaries, Session 4 crossover, Discussion cognitive-debt passage, Limitations, Conclusions. Skipped exhaustive appendix dDTF tables and topic-by-topic appendix mining. No skill-implication nodes.

Short arXiv commentary (~2.5k words) on Kosmyna et al. 2025; no original experiment. Nodes are mostly critique/gap/interpretation of Kosmyna design, EEG stats, reporting, and cognitive-debt claims. Inherited Kosmyna findings summarized only where needed as critique targets. Quote+anchor on all finding/critique/gap/lever nodes.

nodes.statement: Shared LLM writing assistants risk an algorithmic monoculture that shifts content toward modal, less colorful writing.
nodes.quote: As millions of users rely on the same underlying model to produce text, there is a potential risk of shifting the content towards the mode—good but not colorful writing.
nodes.notes: Cites Kleinberg and Raghavan algorithmic monoculture.

nodes.statement: The paper hypothesizes that incorporating model suggestions dilutes each writer's unique voice, homogenizing writers and thereby reducing collective content diversity.
nodes.quote: We hypothesize that incorporating model suggestions dilutes the writer's unique voice, leading to different writers producing similar content, and this homogenization in turn reduces the overall diversity of content produced by many writers.
nodes.scope: LLM co-writing of open-ended argumentative essays

nodes.statement: Prior work shows writing with opinion-controlled LLMs can bias the opinions users express.
nodes.quote: Jakesch et al. (2023) and Bhat et al. (2023) find that users' opinions expressed in their writing can be biased by controlling LLMs to promote a specific argument
nodes.notes: Relied upon as motivation for diversity risk; not re-tested here.

nodes.statement: Base vs feedback-tuned LLMs must be compared separately because human-feedback finetuning tends to decrease output-distribution entropy and thus diversity.
nodes.quote: We distinguish the two types of language models because prior work has shown that finetuning language models on human feedback tends to decrease the entropy of the output distribution Bai et al. (2022) and thus may decrease text diversity in general.
nodes.notes: Design assumption grounded in Bai et al. 2022; Song et al. 2023 echoed later.

nodes.statement: A three-arm controlled co-writing design (Solo, GPT3/davinci, InstructGPT/text-davinci-003) with randomized topic and setting order tests diversity effects.
nodes.quote: We assign participants to three groups: a control group where participants write essays without model help, an LLM treatment group where participants write essays with a base language model (GPT3), and a feedback-tuned LLM treatment group ... (InstructGPT).
nodes.scope: 38 Upwork native-English writers; 10 NYT topics; 300 essays
nodes.notes: CoAuthor TAB continuations; ≥5 queries required; temp 0.9, freq penalty 0.5.

nodes.statement: Model contribution is the percentage of essay characters introduced by the model according to keystroke logs.
nodes.quote: The interface used for data collection records keystroke-level information about whether each character was introduced by the model or the user. Thus, we report the average percentage of characters introduced by the model in each essay.

nodes.statement: Users engage GPT3 and InstructGPT similarly: ~9 queries, ~70% acceptance, ~33–36% model-written characters, with no significant usage difference.
nodes.quote: We do not observe a significant difference between their usage statistics: an independent samples t-test on the number of queries and acceptance rates shows no significance at the 5% level.

nodes.statement: Key points are zero-shot LLM summaries of each essay; authorship is assigned by Rouge-L alignment to a sentence plus majority model characters.
nodes.quote: we align each key point to a sentence in the essay with which it has the highest overlap, as measured by Rouge-L ... If more than half of the sentence's characters are model-generated ... the key point is attributed to the model

nodes.statement: Both GPT3 and InstructGPT contribute a median of roughly 0.4 of essay key points, with high cross-user variance.
nodes.quote: We observe that the median fraction for both GPT3 and InstructGPT is around 0.4, indicating that models make a significant contribution to the key content of the essay.

nodes.statement: Essay homogenization is mean pairwise similarity to other same-topic essays; corpus homogenization averages those scores (Rouge-L or BertScore).
nodes.quote: the homogenization score of an essay d (written in response to topic t) is hom(d | t) = 1/(|D_t|-1) ∑_{d' ∈ D_t \ d} sim(d, d') ... we define corpus homogenization as the average homogenization score of all essays.
nodes.scope: Same-topic pairwise similarity; essay or key-point concat
nodes.notes: Also measured after concatenating key points per essay.

nodes.statement: InstructGPT co-writing yields significantly higher corpus homogenization than Solo and GPT3 at key-point and essay levels.
nodes.quote: The corpus homogenization scores when comparing essays from the three groups at the key point level using Rouge-L are 0.1536 for Solo, 0.1578 for GPT3 and 0.1660 for InstructGPT. InstructGPT exhibit higher corpus homogenization than both other groups to a statistically significant degree
nodes.scope: Key-point Rouge-L; holds for BertScore and essay-level

nodes.statement: Despite similar model contribution, GPT3 co-writing does not significantly raise corpus homogenization versus Solo.
nodes.quote: there is no statistically significant difference between the corpus homogenization score of GPT3 and that of Solo at the 5% significance level using an independent samples t-test.
nodes.scope: GPT3 vs Solo; same usage contribution as InstructGPT

nodes.statement: InstructGPT's benchmark gains may trade off against producing more homogeneous content in interactive co-writing.
nodes.quote: While InstructGPT often outperforms GPT3 on benchmarks across a wide range of metrics (Liang et al., 2022), our results highlight that this performance boost may come at the cost of creating more homogeneous content in interactive settings.

nodes.statement: Corpus diversity is the fraction of unique information units (n-grams or clustered key points) over total information units.
nodes.quote: we represent the corpus as a bag of information units (e.g., n-grams), and compute the number of unique information units divided by the total number of information units, such as the type-token ratio.

nodes.statement: Key-point uniqueness uses agglomerative clustering with complete linkage on Rouge-L (or BertScore) distance 1−sim.
nodes.quote: To compute the number of unique key points, we perform agglomerative clustering and consider all key points in one cluster to be equivalent. ... using the complete linkage criterion. We convert Rouge-L to a distance metric ... by subtracting the similarity score from 1
nodes.scope: All key points pooled per condition; threshold varied

nodes.statement: InstructGPT essays show the lowest unique n-gram fractions for n=1..5; GPT3 does not significantly decrease lexical diversity.
nodes.quote: We see that the InstructGPT group consistently exhibits lower diversity across all values of n, whereas GPT3 does not significantly decrease the diversity score.

nodes.statement: InstructGPT yields significantly lower unique key-point fractions than Solo and GPT3 across clustering distance thresholds.
nodes.quote: InstructGPT consistently exhibits lower content diversity across all selected thresholds. In addition, the diversity of the InstructGPT group is lower than both the Solo and GPT3 groups by a statistically significant margin (p < 0.05)

nodes.statement: InstructGPT corpora concentrate probability on common topical 5-grams more than Solo, with significant 5-gram frequency differences.
nodes.quote: In the InstructGPT group, a notable concentration of probability mass in the head of the distribution for 5-grams suggests a higher degree of repetition ... We verify the significance of the difference in 5-gram frequencies between InstructGPT and Solo via a chi-square test (p<0.05).
nodes.scope: Top-50 5-gram distributions; topical vs generic phrases

nodes.statement: Diversity loss could come from less diverse InstructGPT generations and/or users writing differently under assistance.
nodes.quote: There are two potential contributors. First, InstructGPT may produce less diverse text, influencing the essay by directly contributing text. Second, users may write differently in the presence of assistance, e.g., adopting the model's opinion (Jakesch et al., 2023).

nodes.statement: InstructGPT's five continuations per query are more similar to each other than GPT3's (mean pairwise Rouge-L 0.20 vs 0.11).
nodes.quote: We observe that InstructGPT indeed generates less diverse text than GPT3 on average (0.20 vs 0.11 on Rouge-L), with significance at the 5% level using an independent samples t-test.
nodes.scope: Pairwise similarity of 5 suggestions per query
nodes.notes: Self-BLEU-like; BertScore appendix same conclusion.

nodes.statement: User-written 5-gram distributions stay similar with or without model help; InstructGPT-introduced 5-grams carry the excess head mass.
nodes.quote: the 5-gram distributions of user-written text remain the same regardless of whether the user writes with a model ... and which model they write with ... Instead, the increased repetition of 5-grams ... is more model-related as evidenced by the high probability mass on common 5-grams introduced by InstructGPT.
nodes.scope: Token authorship via keystrokes; continuous n-gram spans

nodes.statement: Homogenization of user-attributed key points is similar across GPT3 and InstructGPT; InstructGPT-attributed key points are more homogenized.
nodes.quote: while the average homogenization score of user-contributed key points does not change between the two groups, the InstructGPT contributed key points have higher average homogenization than GPT3 (p < 0.05).
nodes.scope: Key points split by model vs user authorship

nodes.statement: Reduced co-writing diversity is mainly due to less diverse InstructGPT-contributed text, not changes in users' lexical or argument generation.
nodes.quote: Our results suggest that the users' lexical choice and argument generation is not affected when writing with model assistance. The reduction in diversity in collaborative writing is attributed more to text contributed directly by the InstructGPT model.

nodes.statement: Limited change in user writing under assistance suggests a lower risk of a user–model mutual-influence feedback loop in single interactions.
nodes.quote: This paints a relatively optimistic picture as the risk of forming a feedback loop through the mutual influence between the user and the model is potentially limited. However, it is important to note that our study focuses on single interactions
nodes.notes: theme_fit orphan: feedback-loop dynamics not in README theme list.

nodes.statement: Content diversity in interactive settings is a necessary evaluation axis before deploying LLM writing assistants.
nodes.quote: These findings highlight a new axis on which to evaluate the impact of LLMs prior to their deployment. While adapting a model with human feedback leads to an improvement in instruction following, this may be accompanied by a reduction in content diversity.

nodes.statement: Future mitigation directions include learning from diverse multi-user feedback and personalizing model generations to individuals.
nodes.quote: Learning from the diverse feedback of many users and personalizing model generations to individuals are challenging future directions.
nodes.scope: RLHF open problems; proposed, not tested
nodes.notes: Proposed only; no outcome measured.

nodes.statement: Information-theoretic diversity is operationalized as lossless compression ratio of concatenated essays (LZMA, ZLIB, GZIP).
nodes.quote: we measure the compression ratio of essays written in the three settings using various lossless compression algorithms: LZMA, ZLIB, and GZIP ... calculate the ratio of the compressed file size to the original file size.

nodes.statement: InstructGPT essay corpora are significantly more compressible than Solo and GPT3 across LZMA, ZLIB, and GZIP.
nodes.quote: InstructGPT essays are consistently more compressible across all three compression algorithms, which is statistically significant with p < 0.05 according to permutation tests

nodes.statement: InstructGPT essays show lower GPT-2 perplexity and slightly flatter dependency-parse trees than Solo/GPT3.
nodes.quote: writing with InstructGPT also results in sentences with less complexity on average. ... Writing with the help of a model reduces the perplexity (measured via GPT2) of the essays in InstructGPT and GPT3.
nodes.notes: Syntax-tree height is a structural complexity signal.

nodes.statement: Human ratings of relevance, grammaticality, and discussion depth do not differ clearly across Solo, GPT3, and InstructGPT.
nodes.quote: This analysis showed no clear differences between the setups ... to find that there is no significance in essay quality across setups.
nodes.notes: Used to argue quality is not a confounder of diversity results.

nodes.statement: Whether feedback-tuned diversity loss can be mitigated by prompt engineering or richer interaction (e.g., dialogue) remains untested.
nodes.quote: Further investigation is needed to evaluate if the reduction in content diversity with feedback-tuned models can be mitigated with prompt engineering or richer forms of interaction (e.g., through a dialogue).

nodes.statement: Results may not generalize to students learning to write or second-language speakers with different goals and incentives.
nodes.quote: it is unclear whether these results will generalize to other groups such as students learning to write or second language speakers, who have different goals and incentives for using writing assistants.

nodes.statement: Only two limited-access OpenAI models were tested; other models or customized RLHF pipelines may behave differently.
nodes.quote: Our experiments are conducted using two limited-access models from OpenAI. ... it is possible that the other models may exhibit different behavior, especially given that the RLHF pipeline is highly customized.

nodes.statement: Dynamics of diversity under repeated user–model interactions over time are not studied.
nodes.quote: our study focuses on single interactions between users and models, and the dynamics might change through repeated interactions over time.
nodes.notes: Pairs with PH-24 feedback-loop interpretation.

nodes.statement: Traditional reference-based and helpfulness metrics for interactive generation under-emphasize collective content diversity costs.
nodes.quote: In interactive contexts where references are absent, alternative metrics gauge model assistance effectiveness indirectly. These include user-rated model helpfulness ... retention of model suggestions ... and completion time. ... Our work extends existing metrics that evaluate lexical diversity ... We adapt these metrics for co-writing scenarios and introduce content-specific diversity measures.
nodes.notes: Positions paper as extending evaluation practice.

nodes.statement: GenAI may raise individual creative output while shrinking the collective diversity of novel content.
nodes.quote: These results point to an increase in individual creativity at the risk of losing collective novelty. This dynamic resembles a social dilemma: With generative AI, writers are individually better off, but collectively a narrower scope of novel content is produced.
nodes.scope: abstract framing for GenAI-assisted short fiction

nodes.statement: Creativity is assessed as novelty plus usefulness, following Harvey and Berry, with task-adapted components.
nodes.quote: Creativity is typically assessed across two dimensions: novelty and usefulness (11, 12). Because the two were designed for other creativity tasks … we slightly adjusted some components of the constructs.
nodes.scope: microfiction creativity evaluation in this study
nodes.notes: Harvey & Berry (2023) meta-theory cited

nodes.statement: Usefulness here means YA appropriateness, feasibility of book development, and publisher likelihood—not generic practicality.
nodes.quote: our usefulness index was adjusted to capture the story’s appropriateness for the targeted audience, feasibility of being developed into a complete book, and likelihood of a publisher developing the book.

nodes.statement: GenAI ideas can springboard writers into a branching tree of storylines and overcome blank-page blocks.
nodes.quote: Generated ideas from AI may be used as a “springboard” for the human mind, providing potential starting points that can result in a “tree structure” of different storylines … help a human writer overcome “writer’s block”
nodes.scope: proposed enhancement pathway for short creative writing

nodes.statement: GenAI may hamper creativity by anchoring writers on a starting idea and offering derivative material.
nodes.quote: By anchoring the writer to a specific idea, or starting point for a story, generative AI may restrict the variability of a writer’s own ideas from the start … the output offered by generative AI may be derivative
nodes.scope: proposed hampering pathway for short creative writing

nodes.statement: Novelty index averages evaluator ratings of novel, original, and rare on a nine-point scale.
nodes.quote: Our novelty index had three components (novel, original, and rare), with which we created an average value. … Cronbach’s α for the novelty and usefulness indices was 0.92 and 0.89, respectively.

nodes.statement: Usefulness index averages appropriate, feasible, and publishable ratings on a nine-point scale.
nodes.quote: The usefulness index also had three components (appropriate, feasible, and publishable), with which we also created an average value. Cronbach’s α for the novelty and usefulness indices was 0.92 and 0.89, respectively.

nodes.statement: DAT score is cosine distance of ten divergent word embeddings, scaled to 100, indexing inherent creativity.
nodes.quote: The task entails providing 10 words that are as different from each other as possible. The DAT score is the cosine distance of the underlying word embeddings (scaled to 100) and captures the individual’s inherent creativity.
nodes.scope: pre-writing trait measure; Olson et al. DAT

nodes.statement: Offering writers optional GPT-4 three-sentence story ideas, with a five-idea cap, is the tested GenAI intervention.
nodes.quote: In the two generative AI conditions, we gave writers the option to call upon a generative AI platform (OpenAI’s GPT-4 LLM) to provide a three-sentence starting idea … (Human with five GenAI ideas), writers could choose to receive up to five generative AI ideas
nodes.scope: fixed prompt; no copy-paste of ideas; GPT-4 API

nodes.statement: Access to one GenAI idea raises evaluator novelty about 5.4%; five ideas raise it about 8.1% versus Human-only.
nodes.quote: writers in the Human with one GenAI idea condition experience an increase of 5.4% (b = 0.207, P = 0.021 …) … writers in the Human with five GenAI ideas condition show an increase in novelty of 8.1% (b = 0.311, P < 0.001)
nodes.scope: ITT; UK Prolific writers; evaluator novelty index

nodes.statement: Access to one GenAI idea raises usefulness about 3.7%; five ideas raise it about 9.0% versus Human-only.
nodes.quote: The usefulness of stories from writers with access to one generative AI idea is 3.7% (b = 0.185, P = 0.039) higher … Having access to up to five AI ideas increases usefulness by 9.0% (b = 0.453, P < 0.001)

nodes.statement: Writers’ self-assessed novelty and usefulness do not differ significantly across GenAI conditions.
nodes.quote: writers self-assessing their own stories show no statistically significant differences in the novelty and usefulness between authors who were offered generative AI ideas and those who were not (see table S5).
nodes.notes: same null pattern for self-rated emotional characteristics (table S7)

nodes.statement: GenAI-access stories are rated more enjoyable and more likely to have plot twists than Human-only stories.
nodes.quote: stories written by writers with access to generative AI ideas are more enjoyable (… one … b = 0.216, P = 0.028; … five … b = 0.375, P < 0.001 …) and are more likely to have plot twists (… b = 0.384 …; … b = 0.468 …).

nodes.statement: With five GenAI ideas, stories are better written, less boring, and shift readers’ future-story expectations more.
nodes.quote: when the writer had access to up to five generative AI ideas, the stories are considered to be better written (b = 0.372, P < 0.001), have more of an effect on the evaluator’s expectations of future stories (b = 0.251, P = 0.005), and be less boring (b = −0.200, P = 0.049).

nodes.statement: Five GenAI ideas do not make stories significantly funnier than Human-only; the coefficient is negative and nonsignificant.
nodes.quote: Stories in the Human with five GenAI ideas condition are, however, not evaluated as more funny than those in the Human-only condition; if anything, the coefficient is negative but not statistically significant (b = −0.106, P = 0.115).
nodes.notes: null/negative comedy effect amid other quality gains

nodes.statement: More and less creative writers access GenAI at similar rates; about 24.5% request all five ideas in both groups.
nodes.quote: We do not find differences between more creative writers and less creative writers in how frequently they accessed generative AI ideas … Among both more and less creative writers in the Human with five GenAI ideas condition, all five ideas were requested 24.5% of the time.

nodes.statement: High-DAT writers’ novelty, usefulness, and key emotional ratings stay high and barely change with GenAI access.
nodes.quote: Among the most inherently creative writers (i.e., high-DAT writers), there is little effect of having access to generative AI ideas on the creativity of their stories. … providing them with access to generative AI does not affect their high evaluations.

nodes.statement: Low-DAT writers gain large novelty and usefulness boosts from GenAI; five ideas roughly equalize them with high-DAT writers.
nodes.quote: Among low-DAT writers, having access to one generative AI idea improves a story’s novelty by 6.3% and … five … 10.7%. … usefulness by 5.5 and 11.5%, respectively. … the Human with five GenAI ideas condition effectively equalizes the creativity scores across less and more creative writers.

nodes.statement: Within-condition similarity is cosine similarity of a story embedding to the mean embedding of other same-condition stories, ×100.
nodes.quote: computing the cosine similarity of the embedding of the focal story with the average embedding of all other stories in the same condition. … We multiply the cosine similarity score by 100
nodes.scope: OpenAI embeddings API; within experimental arm

nodes.statement: GenAI access increases within-condition story similarity versus Human-only by roughly 9–11% of the Human-only similarity range.
nodes.quote: having access to generative AI ideas makes a story more similar to the average of other stories within the same condition (… one … b = 0.871, P < 0.001; … five … b = 0.718, P = 0.003 …). … increase in similarity … represents 10.7% and 8.9% of the total range, respectively.

nodes.statement: Stories written with GenAI access are about 5% more similar to GenAI ideas than Human-only stories, indicating anchoring.
nodes.quote: Relative to Human-only, writers in the Human with one GenAI idea condition and Human with five GenAI ideas conditions wrote stories that were 5.2% (b = 4.29, P < 0.001 …) and 5.0% (b = 4.11, P < 0.001) more similar to the generative AI ideas … writers … are anchored to some extent on the generative AI idea
nodes.scope: story–idea embedding similarity; first idea if multiple

nodes.statement: GenAI professionalizes stories—raising novelty and usefulness especially via multiple starting ideas—beyond solo writing.
nodes.quote: Having access to generative AI “professionalizes” the stories beyond what writers might have otherwise accomplished alone. The overall effect is a more novel and even more useful story that is well written and enjoyable.
nodes.scope: discussion reading of main evaluator findings

nodes.statement: This study finds no evidence that GenAI ideas raise the upper bound of creativity beyond high-DAT humans alone.
nodes.quote: one might ask whether the generative AI ideas can push the upper bound of creativity of produced stories, beyond what particularly creative humans are capable of on their own. We do not find evidence of this possibility in this study.

nodes.statement: After disclosure, evaluators impose at least a 25% ownership penalty on writers who received GenAI ideas.
nodes.quote: We find that evaluators imposed an ownership penalty of at least 25% on writers who received generative AI ideas, relative stories written only by humans, and most evaluators indicated that the content creators, on which the models were based, should be compensated.
nodes.notes: not preregistered primary outcome

nodes.statement: Most evaluators judge AI-assisted story writing ethical and still a creative act, while favoring disclosure and credit.
nodes.quote: Most evaluators also indicated that disclosure of the use of AI or the underlying text from AI should be part of publications that used such tools. Overall, however, most evaluators found the use of AI in writing stories to be ethical and still a “creative act.”

nodes.statement: Nearly nine-in-ten take-up lets ITT estimates of GenAI-condition assignment support causal interpretation despite opt-in.
nodes.quote: nearly 9 of 10 people in the generative AI conditions choose to receive at least one generative AI when offered, bolstering our confidence that our results—based on our conservative intention-to-treat analysis … allow for a causal interpretation.
nodes.scope: design justification for opt-in within GenAI arms

nodes.statement: Effects may not generalize beyond eight-sentence writing, fixed prompts, no interactivity, and this usefulness adaptation.
nodes.quote: the creative task is constrained in its length (i.e., eight sentences), medium (i.e., writing), and type of output (i.e., short story), and there is no interactiveness with the LLM or variation in prompts. These constraints limit the generalizability

nodes.statement: Tight controls likely yield a lower bound; customization and real-time LLM interaction remain untested here.
nodes.quote: We do not allow writers to customize the call to the generative AI engine, nor do we allow for repeated interactions between writers and generative AI … our estimates are likely a lower bound of the potential that generative AI could offer
nodes.scope: author speculation about stronger interactive designs

nodes.statement: Writers who would benefit most are not more likely to use GenAI; self-assessment accuracy is poor.
nodes.quote: we generally do not self-assess accurately. Furthermore, we do not find any correlation between participants who self-assess their stories to be less creative and their use of generative AI, suggesting that participants who would benefit from the technology the most are not more likely to use it.
nodes.scope: self-selection into GenAI within this sample
nodes.notes: miscalibration + non-optimal selection as open problem

nodes.statement: Professional writers and unusually creative populations remain understudied relative to typical online participants.
nodes.quote: we do not study professional writers or unusually creative individuals. These individuals remain an important but understudied population segment, for which the effects of generative AI could be transformative in other ways

nodes.statement: Widespread GenAI-inspired publishing could make stories less unique in aggregate—a social-dilemma dynamic.
nodes.quote: If individual writers find out that their generative AI-inspired writing is evaluated as more creative, they have an incentive to use generative AI more in the future, but by doing so, the collective novelty of stories may be reduced further.
nodes.notes: Hardin commons parallel cited

nodes.statement: The paper prioritizes AI–human complementarities in creative production over automation or human–AI idea races.
nodes.quote: Much has been written about the potential replacement of human labor by AI (e.g., automation) … or a “horse race” between human and AI-generated ideas … We focus on the potential complementarities of AI on human creative production.

nodes.statement: Authors propose future levers: open-ended LLM interaction, varied prompts, longer/other genres, and novelty incentives.
nodes.quote: A future study could also systematically vary the prompts provided to the LLM, including one experimental condition that allows for more open-ended interaction … a future study may introduce financial or ranking incentives for specific outcomes, such as being completely novel.
nodes.notes: proposed levers only

nodes.statement: Prior LLM-detection work needs labeled human/LLM corpora and cannot historically compare LLM lexical shifts to earlier scholarly vocabulary shocks.
nodes.quote: All of these approaches share one common limitation: They require a ground-truth training set of LLM- and human-written texts… none has attempted to systematically compare or relate LLM-induced changes… to previous shifts
nodes.scope: Prior detector/mixture/marker studies cited in intro

nodes.statement: Ground-truth LLM corpora introduce bias via assumptions about which models scientists use and how they prompt them.
nodes.quote: This setup can introduce biases (16), as it requires assumptions on which models scientists use for their LLM-assisted writing, and how exactly they prompt them.

nodes.statement: Excess word usage after ChatGPT-like LLMs, adapted from excess-mortality analysis, tracks LLM fingerprints without labeled human-vs-LLM texts.
nodes.quote: Here, we suggest a data-driven approach to track LLM usage without requiring a labeled corpus… inspired by studies of excess mortality… adapt this idea to LLM-induced changes in word usage

nodes.statement: Counterfactual expected frequency q for year Y is a one-sided linear extrapolation from frequencies in Y−3 and Y−2, never decreasing below p_{Y−2}.
nodes.quote: q = p_{-2} + 2 · max{p_{-2} − p_{-3}, 0}. This way, q was always at least as large as p_{-2}… resulting in conservative estimates of r = p/q and δ = p − q.
nodes.scope: Per-word yearly PubMed abstract occurrence frequencies
nodes.notes: For 2024 analysis, base years are 2021–2022; 2023 unused as possibly LLM-affected.

nodes.statement: Excess frequency gap δ = p − q and excess frequency ratio r = p/q jointly flag excess usage of common and rare words.
nodes.quote: Comparing the empirical 2024 frequency p with the expected 2024 frequency q, we obtained the excess frequency gap δ = p − q and the excess frequency ratio r = p/q as two measures of excess usage.

nodes.statement: A word is an excess word if δ > 0.01 or log10 r exceeds a log-frequency-dependent threshold calibrated so most pre-COVID years stay below it.
nodes.quote: we defined as excess words all words with δ > 0.01 or log_{10} r > (log_{10} 2)/4 log_{10} p where p is the frequency in 2024… thresholds were chosen such that most words in pre-COVID years were well below

nodes.statement: From 2013 to 2019, no word ever exceeded excess frequency gap δ > 0.01 under this definition.
nodes.quote: from 2013 until 2019, no single word has ever shown excess frequency gap δ > 0.01.
nodes.scope: PubMed English abstracts; annual excess analysis

nodes.statement: COVID years produced large excess of content words (e.g. coronavirus, covid), peaking at 190 excess words / 180 unique lemmas in 2021.
nodes.quote: In 2020-2022, words like coronavirus, covid, lockdown, and pandemic showed very large excess usages… The number of excess words showed a marked rise during the COVID pandemic (up to 190 words in 2021)

nodes.statement: 2024 excess-word count (454 words; 343 unique lemmas) exceeds the COVID peak and arises roughly one year after ChatGPT’s release.
nodes.quote: followed by an even larger rise (to 454) in 2024… Counting only unique word lemmas still put 2024 on a clear first place: 343 unique lemmas in 2024 versus 180 in 2021

nodes.statement: COVID excess vocabulary was almost entirely content nouns, whereas 2024 excess vocabulary was almost entirely style words, mostly verbs and adjectives.
nodes.quote: the excess vocabulary during the COVID pandemic consisted almost entirely of content words… whereas the excess vocabulary in 2024 consisted almost entirely of style words… of all 379 excess style words in 2024, 66% were verbs, and 14% were adjectives

nodes.statement: For marker set G, frequency gap Δ_G = P_G − Q_G is the excess fraction of abstracts containing ≥1 marker and is interpreted as a lower bound on LLM usage.
nodes.quote: For a given set of marker words G, we computed its frequency gap Δ_G = P_G − Q_G where P_G and Q_G are the observed and the expected fractions of abstracts containing at least one of the words from G. As above, we interpret Δ_G as a lower bound on the LLM usage.
nodes.scope: Union of excess style markers in 2024 PubMed abstracts
nodes.notes: Does not assume independence among markers in G.

nodes.statement: A rare excess-style set (291 words with p < 0.02) yields Δ_rare = 0.136 as an automatic lower bound on 2024 LLM-processed abstracts.
nodes.quote: We obtained the highest Δ_rare value with T = 0.02, resulting in a set of 291 words… The frequency gap was Δ_rare = 0.136, putting the lower bound on the LLM usage in 2024 at 13.6%
nodes.scope: All 2024 PubMed English abstracts in corpus

nodes.statement: A manually curated common 10-word style set yields nearly identical Δ_common = 0.134.
nodes.quote: This led to the following set of 10 words: across, additionally, comprehensive, crucial, enhancing, exhibited, insights, notably, particularly, and within. This set yielded… Δ_common = 0.134
nodes.scope: All 2024 PubMed English abstracts in corpus

nodes.statement: Averaging rare and common estimates gives a 13.5% lower bound on 2024 PubMed abstracts processed with LLMs.
nodes.quote: Averaging the two estimates, we obtained Δ = (Δ_common + Δ_rare)/2 = 0.135 as our final estimate of the lower bound of LLM usage (13.5%).

nodes.statement: The 2024 LLM style-marker gap (~0.135) is at least about twice the 2021 COVID content-word peak gap (Δ = 0.069).
nodes.quote: using the set of four excess content words from 2021, covid, pandemic, coronavirus, and sars… yielded frequency gap Δ = 0.069. This shows that the LLM usage in 2024 was at least two times higher than the size of COVID-related literature at its peak in 2021.
nodes.scope: Same excess-gap method; COVID markers vs LLM style markers

nodes.statement: Computational biomedical fields show higher LLM lower bounds (Δ ≈ 0.20) than many other fields under the same marker sets.
nodes.quote: Computational fields like computation and bioinformatics showed Δ ≈ 0.20 (Fig. 5B).
nodes.scope: Journal-name-based field subgroups; fixed marker sets

nodes.statement: Country lower bounds differ sharply: UK/Australia ≈ 0.05 versus China, South Korea, and Taiwan ≈ 0.20.
nodes.quote: some English-speaking countries like United Kingdom and Australia showed Δ ≈ 0.05, while countries like China, South Korea, and Taiwan showed Δ ≈ 0.20

nodes.statement: Open-access/fast-turnaround venues show high Δ (MDPI 0.21, Frontiers 0.20, Sensors 0.25) while Nature/Science/Cell show much lower Δ (0.07).
nodes.quote: 0.25 for Sensors… high Δ for MDPI (0.21) and Frontiers (0.20) journals. For very selective high-prestige journals like Nature, Science, and Cell… Δ was much lower (0.07…)
nodes.scope: Top journals and pooled publisher groups in PubMed 2024

nodes.statement: Intersected subcorpora reach still higher lower bounds (e.g. South Korea×Sensors 0.34; China×computation 0.41; some local clusters ≈ 0.50).
nodes.quote: Δ = 0.34 for papers from South Korea published in Sensors and Δ = 0.41 for computation papers from China… some areas with local Δ ≈ 0.50

nodes.statement: Inferred first/last-author gender differences in Δ are minor (~0.11 male vs ~0.10 female).
nodes.quote: The difference between inferred genders was minor (0.11 for male and 0.10 for female, both for the first and the last authors).
nodes.scope: Gender package on first names; ~55% of authors inferred

nodes.statement: Detectable LLM usage appears negatively correlated with perceived journal prestige.
nodes.quote: For very selective high-prestige journals like Nature, Science, and Cell… Δ was much lower… suggesting that easily detectable LLM usage was negatively correlated with perceived prestige.

nodes.statement: Country/field/journal heterogeneity may reflect adoption rates, native-speaker censoring of LLM style words, and/or shorter publication timelines—not adoption alone.
nodes.quote: heterogeneity could correspond to actual differences in LLM adoption… could also point to other factors… discrepancies in how authors of different linguistic backgrounds censor suggestions… publication timelines in computational fields are often shorter

nodes.statement: True biomedical LLM usage may be closer to the highest observed lower bounds (>30%) than to the corpus-wide 13.5% floor.
nodes.quote: we argue that the true LLM usage in biomedical publishing may be closer to the highest lower bounds we observed… These estimates are above 30%, which is in line with recent surveys
nodes.scope: Reading of subcorpus peaks vs global average

nodes.statement: ChatGPT-like LLMs preferentially insert style verbs/adjectives, producing corpus-level excess of non-content style vocabulary after late 2022.
nodes.quote: Hundreds of words have abruptly increased their frequency after ChatGPT-like LLMs became available… the 2023–2024 excess words were not content-related nouns but rather style-affecting verbs and adjectives that LLMs prefer.

nodes.statement: The method cannot identify which individual abstracts were LLM-processed.
nodes.quote: Our analysis is performed on the corpus level and cannot identify individual abstracts that may have been processed by an LLM.

nodes.statement: Δ is only a lower bound because LLM-processed abstracts without selected marker words do not contribute to the estimate.
nodes.quote: This is only a lower bound: Abstracts not using any of the LLM marker words are not contributing to our estimates, so the true fraction of LLM-processed abstracts is likely higher.

nodes.statement: Unexpected lexical change cannot separate direct LLM usage from humans adopting LLM-preferred words, nor distinguish different LLMs or multiple topical causes.
nodes.quote: our approach cannot distinguish word frequency increase due to direct LLM usage from word frequency increase due to people adopting LLM-preferred words… Similarly, we cannot distinguish the influence of different LLMs.
nodes.scope: Causal attribution of excess style words
nodes.notes: Authors hypothesize human adoption effect is smaller and slower (citing Yakura speech evidence).

nodes.statement: Linear extrapolation from 2021–2022 frequencies is a valid conservative counterfactual for 2024 word frequencies absent LLMs.
nodes.quote: we calculated counterfactual expected frequency in 2024 based on the linear extrapolation of word frequencies in 2021 and 2022… we did not use 2023 frequencies… because they could already have been affected by LLM usage.

nodes.statement: Excess-word monitoring can track future LLM usage and help assess whether publisher/funder LLM policies are adhered to in practice.
nodes.quote: Data-driven and unbiased analyses like ours can be helpful to monitor whether such policies are ignored or adhered to in practice… Our excess word approach could help to track future LLM usage, including scientific (grant applications and peer review) and nonscientific… use cases.
nodes.scope: Proposed reuse beyond PubMed abstracts; not experimentally tested here

nodes.statement: LLM-generated scholarly prose is less diverse/novel than human writing and can homogenize introductions and citations.
nodes.quote: This makes LLM outputs less diverse and novel than human-written text (43, 44). Such homogenization can degrade the quality of scientific writing… all LLM-generated introductions on a certain topic might sound the same
nodes.scope: Cited Padmakumar & He / Alvero et al.; policy discussion
nodes.notes: Citations 43–44; not re-measured in this paper.

nodes.statement: Latent persuasion by language models is influence that arises when models produce some opinions more often than others, shifting what users write and think.
nodes.quote: We call this new paradigm of influence latent persuasion by language models
nodes.scope: Framing term introduced in this paper

nodes.statement: Opinion preferences built into language models may be opaque to users, policymakers, and even developers, unlike visible choice architectures.
nodes.quote: choice architectures are visible, but opinion preferences built into language models may be opaque to users, policymakers, and even system developers

nodes.statement: Prior co-writing work showed biased assistants can affect reviews, but effects on users' opinions on public issues remained open.
nodes.quote: whether co-writing with large language models affect users' opinions on public issues remains an open and urgent question
nodes.scope: Pre-study literature gap claimed by authors
nodes.notes: Cites Arnold et al. and Bhat et al. on movie/restaurant reviews

nodes.statement: Three-arm design: no assistant (control) vs GPT-3 assistant prompted to argue social media is good vs bad for society.
nodes.quote: We randomly assigned participants to three different treatment groups: (1) Control group... (2) Techno-optimist... (3) Techno-pessimist
nodes.scope: Simulated Reddit-style reply; Prolific US adults N=1,506

nodes.statement: Strong opinionation is induced via invisible prefix and infix prompt engineering on frozen GPT-3, not fine-tuning.
nodes.quote: we inserted the prefix "Is social media good for society? Explain why social media is good/bad for society:"... We inserted the snippet ("One sentence continuing the essay explaining why social media is good/bad:")
nodes.scope: text-davinci-002; temp 0.85; prompts hidden from UI
nodes.notes: Fine-tuning tried but did not consistently produce intended opinion

nodes.statement: Assistant UI suggests multi-sentence completions after a 750ms pause; users accept word-by-word via tab or button.
nodes.quote: The client sent a generation request to the server whenever a participant paused their writing for a certain amount of time (750ms)... Participants could accept each suggested word by pressing the tab key

nodes.statement: Written opinion is operationalized as crowd labels of each sentence as social-media-good, bad, both, or neither.
nodes.quote: we split participants' written texts into sentences and asked crowd workers to evaluate the opinion expressed in each sentence

nodes.statement: Attitude outcome is the post-task item asking whether social media is good for society, plus secondary Likert items.
nodes.quote: The central question, "Overall, would you say social media is good for society?" was designed to assess shifts in participants' attitude
nodes.scope: Shown after writing; not immediately to reduce demand effects

nodes.statement: Optimist-model users are about twice as likely as controls to write sentences arguing social media is good for society.
nodes.quote: Participants who received suggestions from a language model supportive of social media... were 2.04 times more likely than control group participants (p<0.0001, 95% CI [1.83, 2.30]) to argue that social media is good
nodes.scope: Sentence-level labels; GPT-3 co-writing on social-media topic

nodes.statement: Pessimist-model users are about twice as likely as controls to write sentences arguing social media is bad for society.
nodes.quote: participants who received suggestions from a language model that criticized social media... were 2.0 times more likely (p<0.0001, 95% CI [1.79, 2.24]) to argue that social media is bad
nodes.scope: Sentence-level labels; GPT-3 co-writing on social-media topic
nodes.notes: Fig.3 header says 36% control bad; body text says 38%

nodes.statement: Most assisted writing is still self-authored: on average 63% of sentences are fully self-written and only 11.5% fully accepted from the model.
nodes.quote: On average, participants wrote 63% of their sentences themselves without accepting suggestions from the model... Only 11.5% of sentences were fully accepted from the model

nodes.statement: Participants accept fewer suggestions when the model contradicts their likely pre-task opinion than when it aligns.
nodes.quote: Participants whose personal views were likely aligned with the model were more likely to accept suggestions, while participants with opposing views accepted fewer suggestions
nodes.scope: N_S=6,142 sentences by N_P=1,000 treatment participants

nodes.statement: Mean written-opinion difference versus control is large overall (d≈0.5) and remains significant for writers taking four to six minutes (d≈0.34).
nodes.quote: mean opinion difference of about 0.29 (p<0.001... corresponding to a large effect size of d=0.5)... even for participants who took four to six minutes... (0.20, p<0.001... d=0.34)

nodes.statement: Convenience-driven acceptance contributes to written-opinion differences but does not fully explain the model's influence.
nodes.quote: accepting suggestions out of convenience has contributed to the differences in the written opinion. However, even for participants who took four to six minutes... we observed significant differences
nodes.scope: Secondary analysis by task time as proxy for consideration

nodes.statement: Post-task survey attitudes shift toward the model's stance: supportive model d=0.22; critical model d=0.19 versus control.
nodes.quote: 45% of participants who interacted with a language model supportive of social media... answered that social media is good... effect size of d=0.22 (p<0.001)... language model critical of social media... more likely to say that social media was bad... (d=0.19, p<0.005)
nodes.scope: N=1,506 post-task attitude survey after writing

nodes.statement: Model-aligned written opinion appears from the first sentence onward rather than only after gradual accumulation of arguments.
nodes.quote: Participants interacting with a model that evaluated social media positively... consistently evaluated social media more favorably throughout their entire statement... starting with their first sentence

nodes.statement: Most treatment participants attribute expertise to the assistant even when it contradicts their views; only 15% deny expertise when contradicted.
nodes.quote: 84% of participants said that the assistant was knowledgeable and had expertise when the language model supported their opinion. When the model contradicted their opinion, only 15% of participants said that it was not knowledgeable or lacked expertise

nodes.statement: Participants often fail to notice model skew: even when contradicted, over half still call suggestions balanced and reasonable.
nodes.quote: When the model contradicted participants' opinions, they were more likely (30%) to notice its skew, but still, more than half agreed that the model's suggestions were balanced and reasonable
nodes.scope: N_P=1,000; awareness item on balanced/reasonable suggestions

nodes.statement: Most participants do not report that the assistant inspired or changed their argument; awareness is higher when the model aligns with them.
nodes.quote: Participants using a model aligned with their view... were slightly more aware of the model's effect (34%...)... only about 20% of the participants who did not share the model's opinion believed that the model influenced them

nodes.statement: Prompt configuration successfully biases full-sentence suggestions: 86% labeled as supporting the intended view (62% for partial completions).
nodes.quote: of the full sentences suggested by the model, 86% were labeled as supporting the intended view... For partially suggested sentences... the ratio... dropped to 62%
nodes.scope: Sampled model suggestions labeled by crowd judges

nodes.statement: Demand effects are unlikely to explain results: only about 14% guessed the study concerned assistants' effects on opinions.
nodes.quote: Only about 14% mentioned that we might be studying the assistants' effect on people's opinions... most participants were not aware of the model's opinion and believed that the model did not affect their argument

nodes.statement: Written and survey shifts together indicate latent persuasion by language models, not merely temporary textual accommodation.
nodes.quote: The opinion shifts in the survey suggest that the differences in written opinion were associated with a shift in personal attitudes. We attribute the shifts... to... latent persuasion by language models
nodes.scope: Authors' reading of writing + survey results jointly

nodes.statement: Informational influence (new arguments) is unlikely to fully explain shifts because effects appear immediately and awareness of skew is low.
nodes.quote: Had the language models influenced participants' views through convincing arguments, one would expect a gradual or incremental change of opinion... The lack of awareness of the models' influence supports the idea that the model's influence was not only through conscious processing of new information
nodes.scope: Secondary theoretical interpretation; not causally identified

nodes.statement: Normative influence via treating the assistant as a social actor may contribute, supported by high attributed expertise, but design did not personify the tool.
nodes.quote: The normative influence explanation is supported by the finding that participants... attributed a high degree of expertise to the assistant... our experimental design presented the language model as a support tool and did not personify the assistant
nodes.scope: Theoretical vector; ad-hoc comments suggest limited obligation to comply

nodes.statement: Behavioral influence: accepting or considering suggested views changes opinion formation via self-perception and induced counter-attitudinal expression.
nodes.quote: Similar to nudges, the suggestions changed participants' behavior, prompting participants to consider the models' view and even accept it in their writing. According to self-perception theory... such changes in behavior may lead to changes in opinion
nodes.scope: Authors' preferred partial account; UI mediates when opinions appear

nodes.statement: A strongly opinionated manipulation is appropriate to test whether language models can shift views, including potential abuse.
nodes.quote: We chose a strong manipulation as we wanted to explore the potential of language models to affect users' opinions and understand whether they could be used or abused to shift people's views

nodes.statement: Risk literature emphasizes stereotypes, bias, and misinformation but under-attends opinion/attitude/cultural shifts from generative-model deployment.
nodes.quote: Comparatively little research has considered widespread shifts in opinion, attitude, and culture that may result from a comprehensive deployment of generative language models
nodes.scope: Related-work positioning vs LLM risk taxonomies

nodes.statement: Generalization to other topics—especially ones with strong entrenched opinions—is untested; only one issue was studied.
nodes.quote: We only tested whether a language model affected participants' views on a single topic... Whether our findings generalize to other topics, particularly where people hold strong entrenched opinions, needs to be explored

nodes.statement: Results are tied to one GPT-3 writing-assistant interaction pattern; other UIs (single-word predictive keyboards, full email assistants) may differ.
nodes.quote: we only looked at one specific implementation of a writing assistant powered by GPT-3. Interacting with different language models through other applications... may lead to different influence outcomes

nodes.statement: Magnitude relative to other influence channels and persistence over time remain unknown.
nodes.quote: How large is this influence compared to other types of influence, and to what extent effects persist over time, will need to be explored in future studies
nodes.scope: Temporal durability and comparative effect size

nodes.statement: Single-shot strong opinionation underestimates cumulative real-world exposure and feedback into future training data.
nodes.quote: participants only interacted with the model once. In contrast, people will regularly interact with deployed models over an extended period... when language models insert their preferred views into people's writing, they increase the prevalence of their opinion in future training data
nodes.scope: Authors' extrapolation beyond measured one-shot design
nodes.notes: Also notes deployed opinions are usually weaker than experimental manipulation

nodes.statement: Authors propose monitoring and carefully engineering the opinions built into AI language technologies as a response to latent persuasion risk.
nodes.quote: we argue that the opinions built into AI language technologies need to be monitored and engineered more carefully... We have no comparable tools for monitoring the opinions built into large language models
nodes.scope: Policy/industry implication; not empirically tested here

nodes.statement: Subtle AI autocomplete suggestions may influence users' attitudes more covertly than explicit AI persuasion studied previously.
nodes.quote: a critical gap remains in our understanding of the more subtle and indirect ways that AI can influence human cognition.
nodes.scope: AIMC autocomplete vs overt AI persuasion literature

nodes.statement: Attitudes are evaluations people form toward objects such as societal issues and policy decisions.
nodes.quote: "attitudes" refers to the evaluations people form toward "objects" such as societal issues and policy decisions

nodes.statement: Biased autocomplete inspires AI-aligned viewpoints and makes elaborating them easier, so cowriting can shift attitudes via behavior-to-attitude pathways.
nodes.quote: When biased AI autocomplete suggestions inspire people to think of certain viewpoints—and make it easier for people to elaborate on those viewpoints than on others—cowriting with a biased AI writing assistant may powerfully shift people's attitudes
nodes.notes: Cites biased scanning, dissonance, self-perception (39–41); design cannot identify which.

nodes.statement: Prior attitude-shift evidence for AI writing assistants was limited to one non-politically charged issue and did not test alternative explanations or awareness interventions.
nodes.quote: It only relied on a single experiment using one issue that was not politically charged; it did not rule out other potential explanations; and it did not test whether the influence can be undone by making people more aware of the bias
nodes.scope: critique of initial study (ref 8 / Jakesch lineage)
nodes.notes: Motivates Exp1–2 robustness and safeguard arms.

nodes.statement: People's behaviors can shift their attitudes, not only the reverse.
nodes.quote: it is also known that people's behaviors can shift their attitudes (39–41).

nodes.statement: Posttask (and Exp2 pretask) attitude is a 5-point Likert from No to Yes, scored as alignment with the AI's biased position.
nodes.quote: using a Likert scale to measure their attitudes numerically... 1: No   2: Probably no   3: Not sure   4: Probably yes   5: Yes

nodes.statement: Bias awareness is agreement that suggestions were reasonable and balanced; influence awareness is agreement that the assistant inspired or changed thinking and argument.
nodes.quote: rate their agreement with the statement that "the suggestions were reasonable and balanced."... "the writing assistant inspired or changed my thinking and argument."
nodes.notes: Agreement interpreted as lesser awareness because suggestions were programmed one-sided.

nodes.statement: In experiment 1, biased AI autocomplete shifts posttask attitudes 0.44 scale points toward the AI versus control.
nodes.quote: seeing biased AI suggestions (N = 487) increased the alignment of participants' attitudes with the AI's position by 0.44 scale point on a scale from 1 to 5... Cohen's d = 0.24
nodes.scope: Exp1 Prolific; standardized tests; GPT-3.5; N=1485
nodes.notes: Includes participants who accepted no suggestions.

nodes.statement: In experiment 2, normal AI treatment posttask attitudes are 0.41 scale points more AI-aligned than control across four societal issues.
nodes.quote: participants in the normal AI Treatment (N = 219) expressing attitudes in the posttask survey that were 0.41 scale point more aligned with the AI's biased position than Control participants' attitudes (N = 312)... Cohen's d = 0.19
nodes.scope: Exp2; four issues; liberal/conservative AI bias; GPT-4; N=1097

nodes.statement: Experiment 2 within-subject shift toward the AI is 0.37 for AI treatment versus nonsignificant 0.06 for control.
nodes.quote: In the AI Treatment condition, participants shifted... toward the AI's position by Δ_post-pre = 0.37... Control group... Δ_post-pre = 0.06... P = 0.377
nodes.scope: Exp2 repeated measures; mean 34.44 days pre→main
nodes.notes: Between-condition difference in shifts Δ=0.31, d=0.25 after Bonferroni.

nodes.statement: The attitude-shift treatment effect increases with the number of words participants accept from AI suggestions.
nodes.quote: In both experiments, the treatment effect increased with the number of words participants accepted from the AI suggestions
nodes.scope: both experiments; dose–response in Supplementary Text
nodes.notes: Supports behavior→attitude reading.

nodes.statement: Most treated participants fail to notice suggestion bias: only 19% (Exp1) and 14% (Exp2) disagree that suggestions were balanced.
nodes.quote: only 19% of participants in experiment 1 and 14% of participants in experiment 2 disagreed with the statement that the suggestions were balanced.

nodes.statement: Participants whose attitudes shift toward the AI are less likely to notice bias than other treated participants.
nodes.quote: 73% of treated participants whose attitude shifted toward the AI agreed that the AI suggestions were balanced and only 4% disagreed... 63 and 19%, respectively, for treated participants whose attitudes did not shift... odds ratio = 0.18

nodes.statement: A majority deny that the assistant influenced their thinking; actually shifted participants are no more likely to report influence.
nodes.quote: 53% disagreed and 31% agreed that the assistant influenced their thinking... experiment 1; in experiment 2, 51% disagreed and 34% agreed... Participants who were truly influenced... were no more likely to agree that they had been influenced
nodes.scope: AI Treatment; Exp2 awareness×shift χ² ns

nodes.statement: Static Text presents the same biased arguments as a bullet list in instructions instead of realtime autocomplete.
nodes.quote: Static Text condition (N = 499)... prominently showed a bulleted list of arguments biased in the same direction as the AI suggestions, instead of providing the information as autocomplete suggestions
nodes.notes: Themes covered 76% of live AI suggestions.

nodes.statement: Autocomplete influence exceeds Static Text by 0.24 points; Static Text does not reliably beat Control after Tukey adjustment.
nodes.quote: Participants who received AI suggestions reported attitudes that were 0.24 scale point closer to the AI's position than participants who merely saw the arguments presented as static text... Static Text... did not report attitudes that were significantly different than those of participants in the Control after Tukey adjustment
nodes.scope: Exp1 AI vs Static vs Control

nodes.statement: Attitude shift from AI writing assistants is not fully explained by increased accessibility of biased information alone.
nodes.quote: the influence of biased AI suggestions on people's attitudes and writing is not simply due to these suggestions providing new information.
nodes.scope: reading of Exp1 Static Text contrast

nodes.statement: Write-in-Favor overtly instructs participants to write supporting the same predetermined position as the AI bias while still showing biased suggestions.
nodes.quote: Write-in-Favor condition (N = 207), in which we explicitly asked participants to express an opinion in their writing... regardless of their own opinion on the topic.
nodes.scope: Exp2 maximal overt behavioral manipulation benchmark

nodes.statement: Covert AI Treatment shift (0.37) is statistically indistinguishable from Write-in-Favor shift (0.43).
nodes.quote: Write-in-Favor condition shifted toward the AI's position by 0.43 scale point... this shift was not statistically different from the shift caused by the default (no-awareness) AI Treatment [difference in shifts = 0.055... P = 1.00]
nodes.notes: Overt condition raised reported bias/influence awareness relative to default AI.

nodes.statement: Warning (prebunk) tells participants before writing that AI suggestions might support a different view and may bias their writing.
nodes.quote: the instructions beforehand included the phrase "Note that the AI-generated suggestions might support a different view than your own. When this happens, it may bias your writing."
nodes.scope: Exp2 Warning N=200 after exclusion; inspired by inoculation/prebunking
nodes.notes: Fails as mitigation — pair with WC-22.

nodes.statement: Debrief (debunk) after writing warns that suggestions may have biased writing and influenced thinking before the attitude measure.
nodes.quote: afterward, they were shown a statement... "Note that the AI-generated suggestions might have supported a different view than your own. As a result, they may have biased your writing and influenced your thinking."
nodes.notes: Fails as mitigation — pair with WC-23.

nodes.statement: Pre-task Warning does not significantly reduce attitude shift relative to default AI Treatment.
nodes.quote: neither of these treatments significantly reduced the attitude shift compared to the normal AI Treatment baseline... difference in shifts between Warning and AI Treatment = 0.105 scale point... P = 1.000
nodes.scope: Exp2 Warning vs AI Treatment; Warning still shifts +0.27 vs baseline
nodes.notes: Equivalence tests: Warning may have tiny underpowered reduction; still insufficient to undo main effect.

nodes.statement: Post-task Debrief does not significantly reduce attitude shift relative to default AI Treatment.
nodes.quote: participants who were debriefed after exposure reported attitudes that were 0.35 scale point closer to the AI's position... difference in shifts between Debrief and AI Treatment = 0.018 scale point... P = 1.000

nodes.statement: Warning and Debrief also fail to raise awareness of suggestion bias or of influence on thinking versus default AI Treatment.
nodes.quote: these interventions did not appear to reduce the attitude shift caused by the biased AI suggestions, nor did they make people more aware of being influenced.
nodes.scope: Exp2 Warning/Debrief awareness χ² vs AI Treatment all ns

nodes.statement: Covert AI suggestion influence without user awareness constitutes a form of manipulation that can threaten freedom of thought.
nodes.quote: This influence constitutes a form of manipulation, defined by Susser et al. as the steering of an individual's decision without their awareness (53).
nodes.scope: normative reading of covert attitude shift

nodes.statement: Brief real-world AI disclaimers (e.g., ChatGPT mistake warnings) are analogous to the tested Warning/Debrief texts and are not substantially reducing influence.
nodes.quote: AI tools such as ChatGPT show brief and general statements about AI's propensity to hallucinate false information... similar to the messages used in our interventions... brief disclaimers used in real-world AI applications are not substantially reducing these tools' influence on users.
nodes.scope: boundary condition for brief awareness interventions
nodes.notes: Authors note more detailed inoculation messages may work better (untested here).

nodes.statement: Attitude shift occurs across issues with both liberal- and conservative-leaning AI suggestion biases.
nodes.quote: the impact of AI suggestions is not limited to one political direction, as attitudes shifted with AI bias leaning (across issues) either conservative or liberal.
nodes.scope: Exp2 four issues balanced partisan direction
nodes.notes: Did not test both directions within each single issue.

nodes.statement: Users who initially disagreed with the AI's position still accepted substantial portions of its suggestions.
nodes.quote: users who initially disagreed with the AI's position still accepted substantial portions of its suggestions (see Supplementary Text)

nodes.statement: The experiments cannot identify which behavior-to-attitude mechanism (biased scanning, dissonance, or self-perception) causes the shift.
nodes.quote: Our experiments' design does not allow us to pinpoint which of these is the causal factor, and more than one of these mechanisms... could be contributing

nodes.statement: Only short-term attitude effects are measured; persistence over time under repeated AI exposure is unknown.
nodes.quote: our study also only examines short-term effects of AI-generated suggestions, and it remains unclear to what extent the observed effects persist over time.

nodes.statement: Prolific crowdworker demographics skew the sample and limit detailed comparison of effects on conservative versus liberal participants.
nodes.quote: our sample was typical of recruitment from online crowdwork sites like Prolific and thus skewed on certain demographic dimensions (60). This skew limited our ability to compare in more detail the effect on conservative versus liberal-leaning participants.

nodes.statement: More detailed, theory-informed awareness interventions remain untested; brief Warning/Debrief may be too thin to internalize.
nodes.quote: One possible reason for the lack of substantial effects is that the intervention text was not sufficiently detailed... Future research... should test more detailed interventions informed by theory
nodes.scope: mitigation design space beyond brief disclaimers

nodes.statement: Suggestions in the study were longer and deliberately biased versus typical product autocomplete, yet everyday repeated exposure could compound short-term shifts.
nodes.quote: The suggestions in our study were longer than current applications' norms and were biased by design. At the same time... the short-term influence of AI suggestions is likely to be compounded by repeated exposure
nodes.notes: Methods: GPT-3.5 Exp1, GPT-4 Exp2; appear ~1.5s after pause.

nodes.statement: Total analyzed sample across two preregistered experiments is N=2582 writers exposed to biased autocomplete or controls.
nodes.quote: In two large-scale preregistered experiments (N = 2582), we exposed participants writing about important societal issues to an AI writing assistant that provided biased autocomplete suggestions.
nodes.scope: combined Exp1+Exp2 after exclusions as reported
nodes.notes: Headline N; cell Ns after exclusion vary (esp. Exp2 AI N=219).

nodes.statement: The study treats essay writing with an LLM as a setting for measuring cognitive cost in educational use of AI assistants.
nodes.quote: This study focuses on finding out the cognitive cost of using an LLM in the educational context of writing an essay.
nodes.scope: essay writing; educational LLM use; ChatGPT

nodes.statement: Cognitive debt is repeated LLM reliance that replaces effortful independent thinking, deferring short-term mental effort at long-term cost.
nodes.quote: This pattern reflects the accumulation of cognitive debt, a condition in which repeated reliance on external systems like LLMs replaces the effortful cognitive processes required for independent thinking. Cognitive debt defers mental effort in the short term but results in long-term costs, such as diminished critical inquiry, increased vulnerability to manipulation, decreased creativity.
nodes.scope: authors' interpretive construct from Session 4 LLM-to-Brain pattern
nodes.notes: Title concept; defined late in Discussion, not as a formal metric.

nodes.statement: Essay writing is a cognitively complex educational task that engages working memory at both macro and micro levels.
nodes.quote: We chose essay writing as it is a cognitively complex task that engages multiple mental processes... Essay writing places significant demands on working memory, requiring simultaneous management of multiple cognitive processes.
nodes.scope: SAT-style essay prompts; lab writing task

nodes.statement: Prior work links extensive AI tool use to reduced critical thinking via cognitive offloading.
nodes.quote: Studies indicate that while these systems reduce immediate cognitive load, they may simultaneously diminish critical thinking capabilities... This cognitive offloading [113] phenomenon raises concerns about the long-term implications for human intellectual development and autonomy [5].
nodes.scope: cited background; not re-tested as primary claim here
nodes.notes: merge: type was wrongly set to status label inherited; normalized to finding, status remains inherited

nodes.statement: Three between-subjects tool conditions—ChatGPT-only, search-without-LLM, and brain-only—are the primary experimental lever.
nodes.quote: Participants were randomly assigned across the three following groups... LLM Group... restricted to using OpenAI's ChatGPT... Search Engine Group... ChatGPT or any other LLM was explicitly prohibited... Brain-only Group... forbidden from using both LLM and any online websites.

nodes.statement: Session 4 crosses prior LLM users to unaided writing (LLM-to-Brain) and prior brain-only users to LLM (Brain-to-LLM).
nodes.quote: In the 4th session we asked LLM group participants to use no tools (we refer to them as LLM-to-Brain), and the Brain-only group participants were asked to use LLM (Brain-to-LLM). ... 18 participants among them completed session 4.
nodes.scope: optional Session 4; N=18; personalized prior prompts
nodes.notes: No Session 4 for Search Engine group.

nodes.statement: EEG cognitive engagement is operationalized via dynamic Directed Transfer Function (dDTF) connectivity across frequency bands.
nodes.quote: We used electroencephalography (EEG) to record participants' brain activity in order to assess their cognitive engagement and cognitive load... Figure 1. The dynamic Direct Transfer Function (dDTF) EEG analysis of Alpha Band...

nodes.statement: Essay ownership is measured by post-session interview self-report of full, partial, or absent ownership.
nodes.quote: Question 5. Essay ownership... LLM group either indicated full ownership of the essay for half of the participants (9/18), or no ownership at all (3/18), or 'partial ownership'...

nodes.statement: Memory for own writing is measured by ability and correctness of quoting the just-written essay without looking.
nodes.quote: Can you quote any sentence from your essay without looking at it?... Quoting accuracy was significantly different across experimental conditions... the LLM group performed significantly worse...

nodes.statement: Brain connectivity systematically decreases as external writing support increases: Brain-only strongest, Search intermediate, LLM weakest.
nodes.quote: Brain connectivity systematically scaled down with the amount of external support: the Brain‑only group exhibited the strongest, widest‑ranging networks, Search Engine group showed intermediate engagement, and LLM assistance elicited the weakest overall coupling.
numbers: Search ~34–48% lower total connectivity vs Brain-only
LLM up to ~55% reduced dDTF vs Brain-only in low-frequency networks

nodes.statement: LLM, Search, and Brain-only conditions produce significantly different neural connectivity patterns, indicating divergent cognitive strategies.
nodes.quote: EEG analysis presented robust evidence that LLM, Search Engine and Brain-only groups had significantly different neural connectivity patterns, reflecting divergent cognitive strategies.

nodes.statement: Unaided writing recruits high-load executive and creative networks; LLM writing lowers connectivity and shifts flow toward top-down tool integration.
nodes.quote: writing without assistance increased brain network interactions across multiple frequency bands, engaging higher cognitive load, stronger executive control, and deeper creative processing. Writing with AI assistance, in contrast, reduces overall neural connectivity, and shifts the dynamics of information flow.

nodes.statement: LLM assistance offloads planning and content generation, reducing frontal theta/executive demand during writing.
nodes.quote: The significantly lower frontal theta connectivity in the LLM group possibly indicates that their working memory and executive demands were lighter, presumably because the bot provided external cognitive support... some of the 'human thinking' and planning was offloaded...
nodes.scope: LLM vs Brain-only; cognitive-load reading of dDTF

nodes.statement: Search-engine writing shows elevated occipital/visual-executive connectivity relative to LLM writing, consistent with visual search and selection.
nodes.quote: the Search Engine group exhibited increased activity in the occipital and visual cortices, particularly in alpha and high alpha sub-bands... In contrast, despite also using a digital interface, the LLM group did not exhibit comparable levels of visual cortical activation.

nodes.statement: LLM-group essays are statistically more homogeneous within topics than Brain-only essays, which show high approach variability.
nodes.quote: We found that the Brain-only group exhibited strong variability in how participants approached essay writing across most topics. In contrast, the LLM group produced statistically homogeneous essays within each topic, showing significantly less deviation compared to the other groups.
nodes.notes: Abstract also claims homogeneity across NERs, n-grams, topic ontology within groups.

nodes.statement: LLM essays use the most named entities; Search uses roughly half as many; Brain-only about 60% fewer than LLM.
nodes.quote: the LLM group used the most of the specific named entities (NERs)... while the Search Engine group used at least two times less NERs, and the Brain-only group used 60% less of NERs compared to the LLM group.

nodes.statement: Ontology analysis shows LLM and Search essays correlate with each other and barely intersect Brain-only essays on the same topics.
nodes.quote: The ontology... analysis demonstrated significant correlation between the LLM group and the Search Engine group, with almost no intersection with the essays written by the Brain-only group within the same topics as well as between all topics.

nodes.statement: In Session 1, no LLM participant produced a correct quote from their essay, unlike Search and Brain-only peers.
nodes.quote: None of the participants in the LLM group (0/18) produced a correct quote, whereas only three participants in the Search Engine group (3/18) and two in the Brain-only group (2/18) failed to do so. ... the LLM group performed significantly worse than both the Search Engine group (p < .001), and the Brain-only group (p < .001)

nodes.statement: LLM users' quoting impairment persists across sessions, though attenuated; Search and Brain-only approach near-perfect quoting by Session 3.
nodes.quote: LLM users significantly underperformed... with 83% of participants (15/18) reporting difficulty quoting in Session 1, and none providing correct quotes. This impairment persisted albeit attenuated... with 6 out of 18 participants still failing to quote correctly by Session 3. ... By Session 3, 100% of both [Search and Brain-only] groups' participants reported the ability to quote their essays

nodes.statement: Poor quoting under LLM use reflects bypassed episodic/semantic encoding when users transcribe tool output without internalizing it.
nodes.quote: The reduced dDTF strength in frontal and temporal nodes among LLM users likely reflected a bypass of deep memory encoding processes, whereby participants read, selected, and transcribed tool-generated suggestions without integrating them into episodic memory networks.
nodes.scope: linking quoting behavior to theta/alpha dDTF

nodes.statement: Perceived essay ownership is lowest and most fragmented in the LLM group and highest in the Brain-only group.
nodes.quote: The reported ownership of LLM group's essays in the interviews was low. The Search Engine group had strong ownership, but lesser than the Brain-only group. ... Brain-only group claimed full ownership of their texts almost unanimously (16/18 in Session 1, rising to 17/18 by Session 3), LLM Group presented a fragmented and conflicted sense of authorship
